case_info.scenario: A man in his 50s underwent clinical assessment for a 4-month history of recurrent palpitations, fatigue, and progressive exertion dyspnea. He had no history of cardiac disease, and there was no family history of heart disease or sudden death. Physical examination revealed an irregular pulse and a systolic murmur at the heart apex. Holter monitoring and 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings documented irregular narrow-QRS tachycardia in an incessant, repetitive fashion with heart rates up to 180 beats per minute and occasional short runs of wide-QRS tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a dilated and diffusely hypokinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction, 30%) associated with moderate to severe functional mitral regurgitation. Blood test results were within normal limits, including thyroid function, C-reactive protein, and myocardial enzymes. The patient was hospitalized, and medical therapy was initiated, including ACE inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, β-blockers, and diuretics. Coronary angiography revealed no significant coronary stenoses. A representative 12-lead ECG of the arrhythmia is shown inFigure 1.

case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more

Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a dilated and diffusely hypokinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction, 30%) associated with moderate to severe functional mitral regurgitation. Blood test results were within normal limits, including thyroid function, C-reactive protein, and myocardial enzymes. The patient was hospitalized, and medical therapy was initiated, including ACE inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, β-blockers, and diuretics. case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

He had no history of cardiac disease, and there was no family history of heart disease or sudden death. Physical examination revealed an irregular pulse and a systolic murmur at the heart apex. Holter monitoring and 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings documented irregular narrow-QRS tachycardia in an incessant, repetitive fashion with heart rates up to 180 beats per minute and occasional short runs of wide-QRS tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a dilated and diffusely hypokinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction, 30%) associated with moderate to severe functional mitral regurgitation. Blood test results were within normal limits, including thyroid function, C-reactive protein, and myocardial enzymes. The patient was hospitalized, and medical therapy was initiated, including ACE inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, β-blockers, and diuretics. case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to

            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is

            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.
